topics.title: The Brigade System
topics.short: Escoffier organized big kitchens into stations under one chef: chef de cuisine, sous-chef, chefs de partie such as saucier and pâtissier, cooks, commis and dishwashers.
topics.trouble: Learners think every restaurant has the full classical brigade; most kitchens today combine stations.

topics.title: Kitchen Language
topics.short: Short calls keep people safe and orders moving: "behind", "corner", "hot", "sharp", "heard", "fire", "all day", "86" and "on the fly".
topics.trouble: New cooks stay silent when they walk behind someone carrying a hot pan.

topics.title: Station Setup, Prep Lists and Par Levels
topics.short: A par level is how much you need on hand for a service; the prep list is par minus what you have; a station is set up so every item is in reach.
topics.trouble: Cooks prep by habit instead of by par, and run out of one thing while throwing away another.

topics.title: Ordering, Receiving and Inventory
topics.short: Order from pars, check deliveries for temperature, quality and count, rotate stock first in, first out, and count inventory on a schedule.
topics.trouble: Receivers sign for a delivery without checking that cold food arrived cold.

topics.title: Recipe Costing, Yield Tests and Food Cost
topics.short: Usable cost = purchase cost ÷ yield; add up a recipe, divide by portions, and food cost percent = cost ÷ menu price.
topics.trouble: Cooks cost a recipe from the purchase price and forget the trim they throw away.

topics.title: Timing a Service
topics.short: Work backward from the time food must leave the pass; know your ticket times; fire long-cooking items first so a table's plates finish together.
topics.trouble: Cooks start everything at once, so the fast items wait and die under the heat lamp.

topics.title: Cleaning Schedules and Equipment Care
topics.short: Clean as you go, a closing clean every night, and a deep-cleaning schedule; hoods, filters, fryers, ice machines and ovens are cleaned and serviced on the schedule set by the manufacturer and local code.
topics.trouble: Kitchens let hood filters fill with grease, which is a fire risk.

topics.title: Working Safely: Cuts, Burns, Slips and Lifting
topics.short: Prevention habits: sharp knives used with care, dry towels for hot handles, calls when moving, closed non-slip shoes, spills cleaned at once, and help with heavy pots.
topics.trouble: Cooks grab a hot pan handle with a wet towel; water carries heat straight through to the hand.

topics.title: What Michelin Stars Mean
topics.short: Anonymous inspectors award one star ("worth a stop"), two ("worth a detour") or three ("worth a special journey") for the food on the plate, judged on five published criteria.
topics.trouble: People think stars reward fancy rooms and service; Michelin says the stars are for the cooking.

topics.title: Stages, Careers and Certifications
topics.short: Most chefs learn by working, often starting as line cooks; staging (working a short trial), culinary programs, apprenticeships and ACF certification are other steps. Figures from the BLS.
topics.trouble: People think a culinary degree alone makes you a chef; most chefs and head cooks have years of kitchen work behind them.

topics.title: Capstone: Cook a Tasting Menu at Home
topics.short: Plan, cost, prep and cook a five-course tasting menu for four to six people, with a timeline that starts three days ahead.
topics.trouble: First tasting menus try too many new techniques at once; cook each dish once before the big night.
